title: The Makeup Bag Has a Clock—But It Won’t Tell You Everything
subtitle: Open-jar symbols, printed dates and changes in a product can help you make a thoughtful edit. Here’s how to read them without turning one label into a universal rule.
imageAlt: Two friends sit at a bright table, each sorting their own makeup beside a small notebook and a magnifying glass.
imageConcept: Two adult friends at a naturally lit table, reviewing separate makeup bags and reading labels on their own products; a notebook, pen and clean towel make the scene practical rather than clinical.
body: A label is a clue, not a verdict

A makeup bag can feel timeless: the familiar lipstick stays in rotation, the eye palette comes out for occasions, and a few products quietly drift to the bottom. But products have histories, and the packaging may offer useful information—if you know what it does and does not mean. The small open-jar icon, for example, is a Period After Opening symbol. A number followed by “M” indicates the number of months after opening that the product is intended to be used, according to the American Academy of Dermatology Association (AAD). That’s different from a printed expiration date, and neither mark tells you whether a specific item has been contaminated or is safe for every person [1].

AAD says you probably won’t find an expiration date on makeup and that cosmetics in the United States aren’t required to carry a Period After Opening symbol [1]. So a missing symbol is not a secret code—and a number on one product should not become a rule for every mascara, cream or powder. The useful approach is to combine the product’s own directions with a record of when it was opened and what you notice about it.
Make the review personal, not communal

A tidy check works best when everyone handles their own products. If you’re doing it with a sibling or friend, clear a table, put down a clean towel and keep the makeup bags separate. You can compare what the labels say without testing, borrowing or swapping products. That keeps the exercise about reading and organizing—not about judging someone’s routine or deciding what they should wear.

Start by looking for a printed date or specific storage and use instructions. Then find an open-jar symbol, if there is one, and note the number of months shown. If you remember when you first opened the item, write the month and year on a small removable label or in a phone note. If you don’t remember, don’t invent a date: mark it as unknown and consider the rest of the information. AAD suggests keeping track of opening dates, closing containers securely and watching for changes in smell, color or consistency [1]. These are practical ways to understand a product’s history, not a home test that can certify it as safe.
Give eye products their own pass

Separate products used around the eyes before reviewing the rest. Eye-area items deserve particular attention because the area is sensitive and applicators can contact the eye or nearby skin. The FDA advises against sharing or swapping eye cosmetics. It also says to discard eye makeup used during an eye infection. For mascara specifically, manufacturers usually recommend discarding it two to four months after purchase; that is guidance for mascara, not a timetable for every makeup product [2].

If you’re unsure when an eye product was purchased or opened, read its packaging and consider whether you can confidently establish its history. Don’t add water or saliva to mascara to make it easier to use, and don’t pass an applicator between people. These boundaries can be simple and nonjudgmental: each person keeps their own items, and no one has to explain why they choose to keep or discard something. A shared review can make the information clearer while leaving the decision with the person who uses the product.
Look for changes without playing detective

A noticeable new smell, a shift in color, or a texture that has changed can be a reason to stop using a product and check its instructions. A cream that has separated, for instance, may no longer look or feel as it did when new. But appearance is not a reliable way to detect every problem: a product can look unchanged and still have a history you can’t verify. Treat changes as useful warning signs, not as a complete safety test.

Research offers a reason to take product handling seriously, but it should not be stretched into a verdict about an individual makeup bag. A study of donated used cosmetics—including lipsticks, glosses, eyeliners, mascaras and beauty blenders—reported bacterial contamination across the sampled categories, with particularly high average bacterial loads in beauty blenders [3]. The study examined those samples; it cannot tell you whether a particular product in your home is contaminated. Its practical implication is modest: don’t share makeup or applicators, keep containers closed and follow care instructions for tools and products.
Know when the product is more than makeup

Not everything sold in a beauty aisle follows the same labeling logic. Sunscreen is a distinct product category: AAD notes that it has an expiration date, unlike makeup [1]. For sunscreen, follow its labeled expiration date and directions rather than treating an open-jar symbol—or a general makeup rule—as a substitute [1]. AAD’s guidance distinguishes sunscreen from ordinary makeup and advises paying attention to its printed expiration information [1].

This is also why a single “makeup expiration chart” can be misleading. Formulation, packaging, use and product category matter, and labels may give different kinds of information. If the instructions are missing or hard to interpret, look for guidance from the manufacturer or the relevant regulator rather than relying on a date borrowed from a different product. A product’s label is most useful when read in context: what it is, how it is meant to be used, and what its maker says about storage and timing.
A useful sort in four steps

Try this sequence when you have ten or fifteen unhurried minutes. First, group items by use: eye products in one area, other makeup in another, and any sunscreen or treatment products separately. Second, read each label for a printed date, storage instructions and any open-jar symbol. Third, add an opening date only when you know it; if you don’t, record “unknown” rather than guessing. Fourth, note any clear change in smell, color or consistency, then consult the product’s directions before deciding what to do.

Keep only the notes you’ll actually use: perhaps a short list on your phone, or labels on a few frequently used products. Close lids after use and keep tools and containers clean. If a product’s history is unclear, or something about it has changed, set it aside while you check the manufacturer’s instructions. The point is not to turn a beauty routine into an inspection or to throw everything away at once. It’s to make a considered choice with the information you have.

A review can be a small act of care for the things you use—not a demand for a perfectly curated bag. One person may prefer a compact collection they can track easily; another may keep a wider range for different looks, occasions or sensory preferences. Neither approach needs a score. What matters is being able to find the information that applies to each product and make a decision without mistaking a symbol for a universal guarantee.

If you do this with someone else, let the conversation stay generous: ask before offering advice, keep products separate, and leave the final choices to their owner. A clear label, a remembered opening date and an honest note about what you don’t know can be enough to make the next choice easier. The clock in the makeup bag is not one clock at all. It is a set of clues—best read with attention, context and room for individual judgment.
